passage:
In my second year I said yes to everything. The photography club, the debating society, the fest committee, the volunteer group, two friends' projects. Himani asked if I could help with a poster, and I said “Of course!” before she finished. I was afraid of disappointing people, and afraid of missing what everyone else was doing. My planner had a colour for every promise. By the middle of the term, I'd missed a lab submission, arrived late to two meetings, and answered messages half awake. The night before my viva I realised I had prepared nothing. I still remember the sick feeling. Saying yes had felt like kindness, but it was really fear in a friendly voice.
— Lokesh

qa.q: What did Himani ask Lokesh to help with?
qa.a: Himani asked Lokesh to help with a poster.

qa.q: What was Lokesh feeling that made the “yes” come so fast?
qa.a: Lokesh felt afraid of disappointing people and afraid of missing what everyone else was doing.

qa.q: What went wrong as a result of the many yeses?
qa.a: Lokesh missed a lab submission, arrived late to two meetings and had prepared nothing for the viva the night before.

qa.q: How might Himani have felt when Lokesh said “Of course!” before the question ended?
qa.a: Himani probably felt pleased and relieved to get a quick yes, without knowing how full Lokesh's plate already was.

grounding: A student says yes to every club and favour out of fear of disappointing and of missing out, and falls behind on core work.

passage: Faculty adviser's note, Hemant. Preeti came to my office on Tuesday to ask to be added to yet another society, the sixth this term. I checked the attendance sheets: the laboratory course, which Preeti needs most, shows four missed sessions. Preeti cheerfully listed the commitments: the dance team, the quiz club, the fest publicity, tutoring a junior, and a friend's app project. Every one is worthwhile. Preeti said, “How can I say no? They'd be disappointed. And everyone else is doing so much.” Under the smile there was worry. I did not forbid anything. I asked Preeti to write the six on paper and mark which two the laboratory course needs time from, and we agreed to meet next Tuesday.

qa.q: How many societies has Preeti joined this term?
qa.a: Preeti wants to join the sixth society this term.

qa.q: What might Preeti be worrying about under the smile when saying “How can I say no?”
qa.a: Under the smile Preeti feels worry and fear of disappointing others and of missing out.

qa.q: What did Hemant ask Preeti to do instead of forbidding anything?
qa.a: Hemant asked Preeti to write the six commitments on paper and mark which two the laboratory course needs time from.

qa.q: How might Preeti's friends feel if Preeti says no to some requests?
qa.a: They may feel a little disappointed at first, but are likely to understand more than Preeti fears.

grounding: A student joins every club and takes every offer, then falls behind on core work.

passage:
Leela: "Kishore, you're in the drama club, the debate team and the fest committee?"
Kishore: "And I'm helping Arvind move flats on Sunday. And I said yes to that internship interview."
Leela: "When's your statistics assignment due?"
Kishore: "Tomorrow. I haven't started."
Leela: "Why did you say yes to everything?"
Kishore: "If I say no, people think I don't care. And what if the debate team is the thing I'd have loved?"
Leela: "So you're scared of letting people down and scared of missing something."
Kishore: (rubs his face) "When you put it like that..."
Leela: "Which two could you drop?"
Kishore: "The fest committee. And... I'll tell Arvind I can help Saturday for two hours, not all Sunday."
Leela: "And tonight?"
Kishore: "Statistics."

qa.q: When is Kishore's statistics assignment due?
qa.a: It is due tomorrow.

qa.q: Why did Kishore say yes to everything?
qa.a: He was afraid of people thinking he didn't care and afraid of missing out on something he might love.

qa.q: What would you advise Kishore after this talk?
qa.a: Drop the fest committee, limit the help to Arvind, and protect time for core work like statistics first.

qa.q: How does Leela see Kishore's commitments?
qa.a: Leela sees them as overcommitment driven by fear, and helps him name it and choose what to drop.

grounding: A dialogue shows a student who joins everything and helps everyone, falling behind on core work out of fear of disappointing others and missing out.

passage: I'm Ojas, and my first year of college was a buffet I tried to eat all at once. Music club, coding society, NSS volunteering, the college magazine. When Aparna asked me to help with her dance show, I said yes. When a senior offered a research project, I said yes. I was scared of disappointing anyone, and more scared of missing the one thing that would change my life. By November, I had failed a calculus quiz and handed in a lab report two days late. My parents got a letter. I sat on my hostel bed with a list of eleven commitments and circled three. The rest, I apologised for and left.

qa.q: How many commitments were on Ojas's list?
qa.a: There were eleven commitments on the list.

qa.q: What feelings pushed Ojas to say yes to everything?
qa.a: Ojas was scared of disappointing anyone and even more afraid of missing the one thing that might change everything.

qa.q: Which choice helped Ojas recover?
qa.a: Circling three commitments and apologising for the rest put the core work back at the centre.

qa.q: How might Aparna feel if Ojas drops out of her dance show?
qa.a: Aparna might feel disappointed at first, but likely prefers honesty to a helper who is too stretched to show up properly.

grounding: A student recalls saying yes to every club and request out of fear, then falling behind on core coursework.

passage:
Faculty mentor's note, second-year B.Com, October.
Hrithik came to see me after missing his second assignment deadline. He listed his commitments: treasurer of the entrepreneurship cell, volunteer at the blood-donation drive, helping two friends with their projects, and a weekend job his cousin offered. "I couldn't say no to any of them," he said. He was worried about letting people down, and also afraid he'd miss out on something useful for his future. His class representative, Chandrika, had already covered for him at two meetings. We went through the list together. He agreed to step down as treasurer and pause the weekend job until exams end. I will meet him again in two weeks.

qa.q: How many assignment deadlines had Hrithik missed?
qa.a: He had missed his second assignment deadline.

qa.q: What was Hrithik worried about when he couldn't say no?
qa.a: He was worried about letting people down and afraid of missing out on something useful for his future.

qa.q: How did the mentor help, and what could come next?
qa.a: The mentor went through the list with him so he chose to step down as treasurer and pause the job; the two-week follow-up checks it sticks.

qa.q: How is Chandrika affected by Hrithik's overcommitment?
qa.a: Chandrika has had to cover for him at two meetings, carrying extra work because he was stretched too thin.

grounding: A mentor's note shows a student who said yes to everything falling behind on core work, driven by fear of disappointing and missing out.

passage:
Wednesday, 11 pm
Said yes to three more things today. Salma asked if I'd proofread her internship cover letter (sure!). The dance society needs someone to make costumes for the fest (me, obviously). And a senior offered me a paid tutoring slot on Saturdays, and I couldn't turn it down. What if nobody asks again?
Full list now: dance, drama club, NSS on Sundays, tutoring, Salma's letter, and the quiz club I joined because everyone I like is in it.
Then the statistics test results came out. 11 out of 30. I haven't opened the textbook since the second week. Dr Menon wrote "See me" on the sheet.
I sat on the hostel stairs and felt sick. Every single yes felt right at the time. Saying no feels like letting someone down, or missing the one night that matters.
Tomorrow: see Dr Menon. And maybe tell the dance people I can't do costumes.
Yamini

qa.q: What did Yamini score on the statistics test?
qa.a: 11 out of 30.

qa.q: Why does Yamini keep saying yes to everything?
qa.a: Yamini is afraid of letting people down and worried about missing out, so each yes feels right in the moment even as the core work slides.

qa.q: What would you advise Yamini to do first?
qa.a: Keep the plan to see Dr Menon, hand back one commitment such as the costumes, and set aside fixed statistics time before adding anything new.

qa.q: How might Salma feel if she knew what the week looked like?
qa.a: Salma would likely be grateful for the proofreading but also uneasy, and might rather wait for it than have Yamini fall further behind.

grounding: Shows a student who takes on every club, favour and offer out of fear of disappointing people and missing out, then falls behind on core coursework.
